title: Market, Limit and Stop Orders; Slippage and Execution
objectives: Choose between market and limit orders and articulate the certainty each gives up
Compute VWAP fills and slippage when a market order walks through the book
Explain stop-market and stop-limit mechanics, including gap risk and the no-fill failure mode
Apply time-in-force conventions (Day, GTC, IOC, FOK) and basic lot/tick conventions
motivation: An order is the only part of a strategy that actually touches the market. The same idea, 'buy 200 shares', can produce a fill at the touch, a fill a cent and a half worse, no fill at all, or an execution far below your protective stop if the market gapped overnight. Choosing order types deliberately, and measuring what slippage they cost, separates systems that survive from systems that die on execution day.

blocks.text: Market orders: certain execution, uncertain price

blocks.md: A **market order** says 'trade now at whatever the book offers'. It guarantees *quantity* (up to available depth) but not *price*, the price is whatever the market makes it, and your own size can push it. Consider a stock quoted 50.10 bid / 50.12 ask with 100 shares at each touch, and suppose you market-buy 200 shares:

blocks.title: A 200-share market buy, filled level by level
items: First 100 shares fill at the ask: $100 \times 50.12 = $5{,}012.00$.
The next 100 must lift the next level at 50.15: $100 \times 50.15 = $5{,}015.00$.
Ideal cost at the touch would have been $200 \times 50.12 = $10{,}024.00$.
Slippage $= 10{,}027 - 10{,}024 = \$, i.e. 1.5 cents per share against the touch.

blocks.md: **Slippage** is exactly that gap between the price you expected and the price you got, and it has three standard sources: depth consumption (as above), latency (the book moved between your decision and your arrival), and spread (any marketable order pays at least the spread). Measuring slippage per order is standard practice on any serious desk; unmeasured slippage is unpriced risk.

blocks.text: Limit orders: certain price, uncertain execution

blocks.md: A **limit order** names the worst acceptable price. A buy limit at 50.10 executes at 50.10 or better, never worse, but only *if* the ask reaches 50.10. Since the current ask is 50.12, your order simply rests on the bid side of the book, joining the queue at its price level; exchanges fill resting orders in **price-time priority** (best price first, then earliest arrival). You become a liquidity provider: if filled, you typically saved the spread, but you risk never being filled while the price runs away without you. The classic frustration: your limit buys in a falling market and misses in a rising one (**adverse selection of fills**).

blocks.text: Stop orders: conditional triggers, not guarantees

blocks.md: A **stop order** sleeps until the market touches a trigger price, then wakes up as a *market* order. A **stop-market sell** at 49.50 on a position means: once the market trades or bids at 49.50, sell at market, which could be materially below 49.50 if the market is moving fast. Stops do not protect against gaps: if the stock closes at 49.60 and opens at 49.20 on news, the stop activates and your sell fills around 49.20, roughly 30 cents worse than the trigger. The **stop-limit** variant adds a floor: stop 49.50, limit 49.45 means 'on trigger, sell at 49.45 or better', but if the price is already below 49.45 when the order activates, it does **not** execute, and an unprotected position keeps falling. Every stop design trades one failure mode (bad fill) against the other (no fill).

rows: Slippage in thin or fast markets
No fill once price is past the limit

items: **Time in force**: Day (cancels at close), GTC (good-till-cancelled), IOC (immediate-or-cancel: fill what you can now, cancel the rest), FOK (fill-or-kill: all or nothing, instantly).
**Lots and ticks**: US listed equities trade in round lots of 100 shares, with prices on penny ticks (\$0.01 increments for stocks above \$1 per US tick-size rules).
**Sell stops trigger on the bid side, buy stops on the ask side**, a detail that surprises people simulating stops for the first time.

**Marketable limit**: a limit priced through the book (e.g. buy limit at 50.20 when the ask is 50.12) executes immediately at the *better* available price (50.12), a market order with a price cap, often the professional default.

blocks.title: A stop is not an insurance policy
blocks.md: Stops convert into market orders, so in a crash they fill where the market is, not where you hoped. Position sizing and diversification manage crash risk; a stop only manages the ordinary case. And a stop-limit that fails to fill offers *no* protection at all: check which failure mode your system can tolerate.

guidedExercise.prompt: Same quote as the lesson (50.10/50.12, ask size 100 at 50.12 then 200 more at 50.15). You market-buy 300 shares. Compute the total cost, the VWAP, and the slippage versus buying all 300 at the touch.
hints: The first 100 fill at 50.12; the remaining 200 fill at 50.15.
Slippage = actual cost minus (size × touch price).
guidedExercise.solution: Cost $= 100 \times 50.12 + 200 \times 50.15 = 5{,}012 + 10{,}030 = $15{,}042.00$. VWAP $= 15{,}042/300 = \$. Ideal $= 300 \times 50.12 = 15{,}036.00$. Slippage $= \$, or 2 cents per share, it scales with the size you push past the touch.

independentExercise.prompt: You are long 400 shares bought at 122.00 and want downside protection starting at 120.00 but refuse to sell below 119.50. (a) Name the order type and its two trigger parameters. (b) Overnight, the stock gaps down to 119.20. Trace what happens to (i) your order and (ii) a plain stop-market at 120.00, including approximate proceeds on 400 shares for each.
hints: A price floor on a sell combines a trigger with a limit.
independentExercise.solution: (a) A **stop-limit sell**: stop (trigger) 120.00, limit 119.50. (b)(i) The gap puts the market (119.20) below the 119.50 limit; on trigger the order activates but no bid is at or above 119.50, so **it does not execute**, proceeds effectively $\$, position still held, now worth $400 \times 119.20 = $47{,}680$ with no protection. (ii) The stop-market at 120.00 triggers on the open and fills near 119.20: proceeds $\approx 400 \times 119.20 = $47{,}680$, i.e. about \$320 less than the 120.00 trigger would suggest. Both designs take losses in a gap, one via non-fill, one via bad fill; that is the trade-off stop orders always make.

commonMistakes: Assuming a stop executes at the stop price, it becomes a market order and fills at the next available price, possibly through a gap.
Expecting a limit buy at 50.10 to 'catch up' with a rising market: it only fills if the price comes *to* you.
Confusing slippage with commission: commissions are fixed fees, slippage is the price gap created by spread, depth and latency.
Placing stop-limit floors so tight (e.g. limit just below stop) that the order never fills exactly when protection is needed.
realWorldApplication: Execution algorithms (VWAP/TWAP/POV schedulers) slice parent orders into limit pieces to manage slippage; retail brokerages surface stop and trailing-stop types; gaps through stops are a recurring post-earnings-announcement complaint.
quantFinanceApplication: Backtests simulate fills with explicit rules, touch price with depth limits, or VWAP through the book, and report slippage per trade; a stop-loss rule simulated at the stop price instead of the *next* fill price silently overstates strategy performance.
summary: Market orders guarantee quantity, not price; the 200-share example filled at VWAP 50.135, costing \$3.00 of slippage versus the touch.
Limit orders guarantee price, not execution; resting limits earn the spread but face missed fills and adverse selection.
Stops trigger into market (or limit) orders: gap risk means fills below the stop; stop-limit floors risk complete non-fill.
Conventions matter: Day/GTC/IOC/FOK time in force, 100-share round lots, penny ticks, and sell stops triggering on the bid side.

quiz.prompt: A market order guarantees which of the following?
options: Quantity (up to available depth), but not price
quiz.explanation: Market orders execute immediately at whatever price the book offers; size beyond displayed depth fills at worse levels, so price is never guaranteed.

quiz.prompt: You market-buy 400 shares. The book fills 100 at 50.12 and 300 at 50.15. What is the VWAP of your fill, to four decimals (e.g. 50.1425)?
Your stop-market sell at 49.50 is active overnight. The stock closes at 49.60 and opens at 49.20 on bad news. Roughly where does your order fill?
options: Exactly 49.50, because that is the stop price
Around 49.20, the next available price after the gap
The order cancels because the market moved past the stop
quiz.explanation: A stop-market converts to a market order once triggered; after a gap it fills near the open (49.20). Stops do not guarantee the trigger price, that is gap risk.

quiz.prompt: Which statements about a resting buy limit at 50.10 while the ask is 50.12 are true?
options: It joins the book on the bid side and waits for price-time priority
It will execute at 50.10 or better if the ask falls to that level
It can never fill while the price rises
quiz.explanation: A non-marketable limit rests on the book; it fills only if the market trades down to it (at 50.10 or better). While price rises away, it stays unfilled, the certainty/execution trade-off of limits.

quiz.prompt: What does this Python code print?
quiz.code:
fills = [(100, 50.12), (100, 50.15)]
cost = sum(q * p for q, p in fills)
qty = sum(q for q, p in fills)
print(round(cost / qty, 3))
quiz.explanation: Cost $= 5{,}012 + 5{,}015 = 10{,}027$ over 200 shares: VWAP $= 50.135$, matching the lesson's worked example of walking through depth.

quiz.prompt: Define slippage and name two of its standard sources.
quiz.modelAnswer: Slippage is the difference between the price expected when placing an order and the price actually obtained; standard sources include spread, walking through depth (market impact) and latency (the book moving before the order arrives).
quiz.explanation: Any marketable order pays the spread at minimum, more when it consumes depth, and latency turns a good decision into a worse fill.

flashcards.back: Market: execution certain, price uncertain (slippage). Limit: price certain (limit or better), execution uncertain (may never fill).
Stop-market: triggers, then sells/buys at market (gap risk). Stop-limit: triggers, then executes only at the limit or better (non-fill risk once past the limit).
Actual fill price minus expected price. Sources: spread, depth consumption (impact), latency. Measured per order on real desks.
Day (cancel at close), GTC (good-till-cancelled), IOC (immediate-or-cancel: partial fill allowed, rest cancelled), FOK (fill-or-kill: everything now or nothing).
